claim_verdicts.evidence: Mirror, TIP: "Big-O notation describes how the work grows as the collection size, `n`, grows. O(1), pronounced "order one," means the operation takes about the same amount of work no matter how many elements the collection contains. O(n), pronounced "order n," means the work grows roughly in proportion to the number of elements in the collection." "about the same" / "roughly in proportion" is the documented licence to drop constant factors; keeping only the fastest-growing term is part of the notation's definition, not a product behaviour.

Mirror complexity table, columns Mutable | Amortized | Worst Case: "| `Dictionary<T>` lookup | O(1) | O(1) – or strictly O(`n`) |". The claim is hedged ("costs about the same"), which matches the amortized column and the TIP's "takes about the same amount of work no matter how many elements the collection contains". Nothing beyond the documented cost (no bucket mechanism, no timing) is asserted.

Definitional: repeatedly halving n reaches 1 after log2(n) halvings, so each doubling of n adds exactly one step. No product behaviour, version-dependent detail or measured number is asserted, and the ledger kind is `fact`, not `behavior`/`number`/`syntax`.
claim_verdicts.source: mathematical definition of the base-2 logarithm

claim_verdicts.evidence: Source read at stage-0 (NestedLoops.cs l.10-16): the inner `foreach (var customerId in customerIds)` runs in full for every element of `orderCustomerIds`, with no `break`, so the body executes |orderCustomerIds| × |customerIds| times — a product, not a sum. Confirmed by running the sample: two arrays of 1,000 give the printed 1000000, not 2000.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Data/NestedLoops.cs l.6-34 (checkout at stage-0); executed run

claim_verdicts.evidence: db/seed.sql header: "Fixed data for the lab: 8 products, 5 customers (one of whom never ordered), 12 orders." — the INSERTs list customer ids 1-5 and order ids 1-12, and 12 × 5 = 60. For the second number, `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- nested-loops` printed "slow way: 1000 matches, 1000000 comparisons", i.e. 1000 × 1000.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang db/seed.sql l.1-2, l.16-35; executed run of NestedLoops

claim_verdicts.evidence: List<T>.Sort Remarks (defaultMoniker net-10.0), all four overloads: "This method is an O(n log n) operation, where n is Count." Array.Sort Remarks, same moniker: "This method is an O(n log n) operation, where n is length." For OrderBy the mirror's breaking-change page states: "In .NET 5 and later versions ... calling OrderBy or OrderByDescending followed by First or FirstOrDefault operates with `O(N log N)` complexity". No "on average" hedge and no worst-case O(n^2) appears on the net-10.0 Sort pages. Ladder ordering is arithmetic.

TIP: "O(n) ... means the work grows roughly in proportion to the number of elements in the collection." One pass and two passes are both proportional to n, so the notation puts both at O(n). The second half follows from the dropped constants: with costs c1·n² and c2·n, c1·n² < c2·n for every n < c2/c1, so a cheap-bodied quadratic can beat an expensive-bodied linear while n stays small. The lesson states it with that condition ("while `n` stays small").

Ledger kind=opinion, needs_verification=false, and the lesson states it with its reason attached: "The estimate is cheap, because you can do it while reading the code; only the measurement needs a run on real data to separate two options of the same shape." A conditioned working method, nothing falsifiable against documentation.

Program.cs of DonHang.Samples registers `["nested-loops"] = Sync(NestedLoops.Run),` in `var samples = new Dictionary<string, Func<Task>>` and prints usage `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- <sample>`. NestedLoops.Run contains `var orders = Enumerable.Range(1, 1_000).ToArray();` and the same for `customers`. The command dispatched and produced output, so the registration resolves. Read from the submodule checkout: `git` was unavailable in this session, so the tag object itself was not re-resolved; no mismatch was observed.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs l.19, l.29; Samples/Data/NestedLoops.cs l.27-34

claim_verdicts.evidence: HashSet<T>(IEnumerable<T>) Remarks, defaultMoniker net-10.0: "This constructor is an O(`n`) operation, where `n` is the number of elements in the `collection` parameter." The overload summary says it "contains elements copied from the specified collection, and has sufficient capacity to accommodate the number of elements copied" — one pass over the argument. (Same page: duplicates collapse; the sample's ids are distinct.)

Set lookup: mirror table "| `HashSet<T>.Add`, lookup | O(1) [Amortized] | O(`n`) [Worst Case] |" — the claim's condition "as long as the hash codes spread the items out" is exactly what separates those two columns. Count with a predicate: CA1851 ("Possible multiple enumerations of `IEnumerable` collection") exists because a LINQ count enumerates its source; and the executed run returns 1000 matches over 1,000 ids, which requires visiting every element once.

PostgreSQL 17, 11.1 Introduction to Indexes: "With no advance preparation, the system would have to scan the entire test1 table, row by row, to find all matching entries." and "If there are many rows in test1 and only a few rows (perhaps zero or one) that would be returned by such a query, this is clearly an inefficient method." Reading every row row-by-row is the whole of the claim; "grows in step with the number of rows" restates it. The docs do not use O() notation here, and the claim does not either.

TIP: "Big-O notation describes how the work grows as the collection size, `n`, grows." — work, not elapsed time; and O(1) is defined as "about the same amount of work no matter how many elements the collection contains". No duration appears anywhere in the notation as the documentation defines it, so a prediction in milliseconds is outside what it states.

Arithmetic under the documented meaning of O(n) ("the work grows roughly in proportion to the number of elements in the collection"): an inner loop with a fixed bound k executes n·k times, and n·k is a constant multiple of n, hence still proportional to n. No version- or product-specific behaviour is asserted.

TIP: "O(1), pronounced "order one," means the operation takes about the same amount of work no matter how many elements the collection contains." The definition fixes only independence from the element count and says nothing about the size of that work, so a constant-time step may cost more than many cheap ones. The ledger states this with "can be"; see issue on §6, where the lesson drops the hedge.

Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- nested-loops` in examples/don-hang (dotnet --version → 10.0.300). Output, verbatim and in this order: "slow way: 1000 matches, 1000000 comparisons" then "fast way: 1000 matches, 1000 lookups" — character for character what §7 Expected result promises.

From the source: the quadratic method compares once per (order, customer) pair with no early exit, so two arrays of 2,000 give 2000 × 2000 = 4000000 against the 1000 × 1000 = 1000000 the run printed; the linear method asks one `Contains` per order, so 2000 against 1000. Doubling therefore doubles the linear count and quadruples the quadratic one, as the suggested answer says.

NestedLoops.cs l.32-33: `Console.WriteLine($"slow way: {CountKnownCustomersSlowly(orders, customers)} matches, 1000000 comparisons");` — only the match count is interpolated; "1000000 comparisons" and "1000 lookups" are literal text in the format strings. Neither method keeps an operation counter: the quadratic one declares only `found`, the linear one returns `orderCustomerIds.Count(known.Contains)`.

issues.text: The §1 recap asserts indexed-lookup behaviour that no ledger claim covers (claim 12 covers only the no-index half) and that PostgreSQL 17 does not word this way. Ch. 11.1 says the planner "can use a more efficient method for locating matching rows. For instance, it might only have to walk a few levels deep into a search tree." — a tree descent, not a jump straight to the rows. `versions_used` includes postgresql, so the sentence reads as product behaviour.
issues.fix: Reword to "…and stop reading every row once an index existed", which claim 12's evidence already supports. If the indexed case must stay, add a ledger claim sourced to PostgreSQL 17 §11.1 and write "walk a few levels of a search tree instead of reading every row".
issues.quote: jump straight to matching rows once an index existed

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the gloss on where `O(n log n)` comes from. Claim 6 covers only the cost of the library sorts, not this mechanism. For the three APIs named right after it, Microsoft documents the algorithm as introsort (insertion sort under 16 elements, otherwise quicksort, heapsort past 2·logN partitions) — not one pass with a logarithmic step per item. The product n × log n is right; the pass-and-step story is true of a heap build, not of what `List<T>.Sort` is documented to do.
issues.fix: State the shape without the mechanism: "`O(n log n)` — the work is `n` multiplied by a logarithmic step, so it grows faster than `O(n)` but far slower than `O(n²)`; putting a collection in order with the sort the library gives you — `List<T>.Sort`, `Array.Sort`, `OrderBy` — costs this much." Add it to the ledger if the mechanism is kept.
issues.quote: `O(n log n)` — one pass over the input where each item costs a logarithmic step

issues.text: An unconditioned comparative timing claim: one file read is asserted to be slower than a thousand comparisons, with no source and no condition (file size, cache state, comparison type all decide it). Claim 15 hedges — "a constant-time step can be slower than many cheap comparisons" — but the lesson asserts it as fact, and the same wording is repeated in quiz q1 explanation b.
issues.fix: Restore the ledger's hedge in §6: "a single step that reads a file is constant and can easily cost more than a thousand comparisons". Match the wording in the q1 explanation for option b.
issues.quote: a single step that reads a file is constant and still slower than a thousand comparisons
